newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator Lott floats action on chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator Lott floats action on chemical treaty.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, in a letter to President Bill Clinton, has raised the possibility the Senate might act on the long-delayed chemical arms treaty if Clinton also submits two other arms agreements for Senate approval.
The two are a 1996 agreement modifying the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty and two documents affecting the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty.

A Senate Republican leadership aide insisted Lott's letter -- dated Jan. 8 and obtained by Reuters -- did not propose a "deal" to the administration and that none is near. "This is the starting point for discussions," the aide said.
But Lott's letter lays a marker that has given some experts hope that an impasse over the chemical treaty, which bans production, use and stockpiling of nerve agents, eventually can be broken.

Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright hinted at flexibility in meeting Republican concerns in written answers to over 200 questions posed by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee as part of her confirmation process.
The committee is to vote on Monday to recommend that the full Senate approve her nomination to succeed Warren Christopher.
Clinton has begun a push to persuade the Republican-led Senate to approve the chemical pact by the end of April.
National Security Adviser-designate Sandy Berger held talks with Lott last week and later a senior official told Reuters Lott was "open-minded" about letting the pact go forward.
In his letter, Lott said he wanted to work with Clinton but "bipartisanship is a two-way street."

"It will be very difficult to explore the possibility of Senate action on the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) without first addressing legitimate security and constitutional concerns on other important arms control issues," he said, citing administration-negotiated changes to the ABM and CFE pacts.

Lott and other Republicans insist the CFE and ABM changes are so substantial they must be sent to the Senate for a two-thirds vote of approval. The administration, worried Senate opponents could overturn the pacts, has resisted.
Albright restated the U.S. position that the CFE agreement, which lets Russia retain more conventional arms in the Caucuses, "does not constitute a formal treaty amendment."

But she said, if confirmed, "I intend to re-examine on a priority basis with my new national security colleagues the question of how best to secure congressional approval of the flank agreement." She did not rule out Senate action.

On the ABM treaty, which limits missile defences, Albright said an accord expanding the pact to include Ukraine, Belarus and Kazahkstan, as well as Russia, "addresses implementation of an exising treaty and thus does not require Senate approval."

But an accord defining differences between strategic missile defence systems constrained by the treaty and permitted regional systems "would be a substantive change to the obligations of the treaty," she said.

While not promising to put this second ABM modification to the Senate, Albright said: "Once the agreement is completed we will consult closely with Congress before making a decision on how to proceed."

Now that more than 65 countries have ratified the CWC pact, it is due to go into force on April 29, even without the United States. America and Russia, which also has not ratified it, are the only countries to admit possessing chemical arms.

The Senate was to vote on the CWC last September, but a last-minute shift against the treaty by Republican presidential contender Bob Dole led to administration fears it might fail to gain the required two-thirds majority, and the vote was put off.
The treaty is with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, whose chairman, Republican Jesse Helms of North Carolina, is an opponent and has power to prevent it going to the full Senate.
